\section[\gu{હું}]{\gu{હું} (hũ) — \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C03-hun}



\begin{quote}
To answer \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} you first need \textquotedblleft{}I.\textquotedblright{} In the name exchange you learned \emph{mārũ} (\textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}); here is its owner.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{હ}} (\emph{ha}) + the \emph{u}-sign + nasal $\to$ \textbf{\gu{હું}} (\emph{hũ}). One nasal syllable.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{હું}} (\emph{hũ}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) descends from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{અહમ્}} (\emph{aham}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}), worn down through Old Gujarati (\emph{haũ}) to \emph{hũ}. That \emph{aham} is from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}eǵ(H)om} — the ancestor of Latin \textbf{ego} and English \textbf{I}. So Gujarati's \emph{hũ}, Latin \emph{ego}, and English \emph{I} are one ancient word. Its possessive is the \textbf{\gu{મારું}} (\emph{mārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}my\textquotedblright{}) from that name exchange.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} plus the copula}]
\emph{Hũ} takes the copula \textbf{\gu{છું}} (\emph{chhũ}, \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}): \emph{hũ … chhũ}. So the answer to \emph{tame kem chho?} begins \textbf{\gu{હું}} (\emph{hũ …}).
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hũ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the family — \emph{hũ} / Latin \emph{ego} / English \textbf{I}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hũ … chhũ\textquotedblright{} — I am …
\end{itemize}

\section[\gu{કેમ}]{\gu{કેમ} (kem) — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} a proper k- question}

\label{lesson:GU-C03-kem}



\begin{quote}
Where \emph{shũ} (\textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) hid its k-, this one wears it plainly — and it opens the most Gujarati of greetings.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ક}} (\emph{ka}) + \textbf{\gu{ે}} (the \emph{e}-sign) + \textbf{\gu{મ}} (\emph{ma}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{કેમ}} (\emph{kem}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{કેમ}} (\emph{kem}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}; also \textquotedblleft{}why\textquotedblright{}) is from the interrogative stem \textbf{\gu{ક}-} (\emph{ka-}), PIE \textbf{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-} — the same root behind English \textbf{wh-} and Latin \emph{qu-}. It heads the plain \emph{k-} family Gujarati mostly kept: \emph{kem} (how), \emph{kōṇ} (who), \emph{kyā̃} (where), \emph{kyāre} (when). And \textbf{\gu{કેમ} \gu{છો}?} (\emph{kem chho?}, \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}) is, for most Gujaratis, the real everyday hello — warmer than \emph{namaste}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kem\textquotedblright{}
  \item the k- question family — \emph{kem, kōṇ, kyā̃, kyāre}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script retrieval}
Hide the earlier model for \textbf{\gu{ભ}}. Write it once, compare, and stop after one possible repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root does \emph{kem} share with English \emph{how/what}? (The interrogative \emph{ka-}, PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{તમે} \gu{કેમ} \gu{છો}?]{\gu{તમે} \gu{કેમ} \gu{છો}? (tame kem chho?) — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C03-tame-kem-chho}



\begin{quote}
The greeting most Gujaratis actually use — three words you already own.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{તમે} \gu{કેમ} \gu{છો}?} = \textbf{\gu{તમે}} (\emph{tame}, respectful \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{કેમ}} (\emph{kem}, \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{છો}} (\emph{chho}, \textquotedblleft{}are\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{you how are?}\textquotedblright{}, the verb last. \emph{Chho} is the respectful/plural form of the copula \emph{chhe} you met in the name exchange (\emph{hũ chhũ} I am / \emph{tame chho} you are). To a friend (\emph{tũ}): \textbf{\gu{તું} \gu{કેમ} \gu{છે}?} (\emph{tũ kem chhe?}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: match the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} to the copula}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Respectful: \textbf{\gu{તમે} \gu{કેમ} \gu{છો}?} (\emph{tame … chho})
  \item Familiar: \textbf{\gu{તું} \gu{કેમ} \gu{છે}?} (\emph{tũ … chhe})
\end{itemize}

Same pattern as every Indo-Aryan track: the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} and its verb-form travel together.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the respectful greeting — \emph{tame kem chho?}
  \item the familiar version — \emph{tũ kem chhe?}
  \item where the verb sits (at the end)
\end{itemize}

\section[\gu{મજા}]{\gu{મજા} (majā) — \textquotedblleft{}enjoyment,\textquotedblright{} and how to answer}

\label{lesson:GU-C03-majaa}



\begin{quote}
The word that answers \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — and it comes not from Sanskrit but from Persia.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{મ}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\gu{જા}} (\emph{jā}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{મજા}} (\emph{majā}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{મજા}} (\emph{majā}, \textquotedblleft{}enjoyment, fun, relish, pleasure\textquotedblright{}) is \textbf{not} Sanskrit — it is \textbf{Perso-Arabic}, from Persian \textbf{maza} (\textquotedblleft{}taste, relish\textquotedblright{}). Gujaratis, a great trading people, wove thousands of Persian and Arabic words into their speech over centuries of commerce across the Arabian Sea — and even \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{} is answered with one. To say \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I'm well},\textquotedblright{} Gujarati says \textbf{\gu{હું} \gu{મજામાં} \gu{છું}} (\emph{hũ majāmā chhũ}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I am in enjoyment}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{majā} + \emph{-mā} \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} + \emph{chhũ} \textquotedblleft{}am\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{The exchange — the reply}
\begin{quote}
— \emph{tame kem chho?} (\textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{majāmā, ābhār.} (\textquotedblleft{}Well {[}lit. 'in enjoyment'{]}, thank you.\textquotedblright{})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}majā\textquotedblright{}
  \item the full reply — \emph{hũ majāmā chhũ}
  \item which heritage \emph{majā} belongs to (Persian, not Sanskrit)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script retrieval}
Hide the earlier model for \textbf{\gu{ૃ}}. Write the below-consonant sign once, compare, and stop after one possible repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{વાંધો} \gu{નહીં}]{\gu{વાંધો} \gu{નહીં} (vāndho nahĩ) — \textquotedblleft{}no problem\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C03-vandho-nahi}



\begin{quote}
When someone thanks you — or apologises — this is the easy, gracious reply.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{વાંધો}} (\emph{vāndho}, \textquotedblleft{}objection, problem\textquotedblright{} — with the nasal on \textbf{\gu{વાં}}) + \textbf{\gu{નહીં}} (\emph{nahĩ}, \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \emph{vāndho nahĩ}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{વાંધો} \gu{નહીં}} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}there is{]} no objection}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vāndho} (\textquotedblleft{}objection, difficulty, harm\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{નહીં}} (\emph{nahĩ}, \textquotedblleft{}not / no\textquotedblright{}). It serves as \textquotedblleft{}it's okay / no worries / no problem / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} The negative \textbf{\gu{નહીં}} (\emph{nahĩ}) is the fuller form of the \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}) from the earlier yes/no lesson — both from the ancient \textbf{na-}, Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*ne}, behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, and Hindi \emph{nahīṁ}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vāndho nahĩ\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}no objection\textquotedblright{})
  \item the exchange — \emph{ābhār} / \emph{vāndho nahĩ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{vāndho nahĩ} literally say, and what ancient root is its \emph{nahĩ} from? (\textquotedblleft{}No objection\textquotedblright{}; PIE \emph{*ne} — English \emph{no/not}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 5 — The how-are-you exchange}

\label{lesson:GU-C03-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The whole responding cycle, from atoms you now own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}How are you?\textquotedblright{} (the everyday hello) — \emph{tame kem chho?}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I'm well, thank you.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{hũ majāmā chhũ, ābhār.}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}No problem / you're welcome.\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vāndho nahĩ.}
  \item the familiar question — \emph{tũ kem chhe?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the k- question-word for \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kem})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} and its copula (\emph{hũ}, \emph{chhũ})
  \item which of your words is Persian, not Sanskrit (\emph{majā})
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kem} $\leftarrow$ the interrogative \emph{k-} (PIE \emph{*k\textsuperscript{w}o-}), cousin of English \emph{how/what}
  \item \emph{hũ} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{aham} $\to$ Latin \emph{ego}, English \textbf{I}
  \item \emph{majā} $\leftarrow$ \textbf{Persian} \emph{maza}, \textquotedblleft{}taste/relish\textquotedblright{} — the trade-language layer
  \item \emph{nahĩ} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*ne}, English \emph{no} (in \emph{vāndho nahĩ})
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Someone greets you with \emph{tame kem chho?} — reply that you're well and thank them. (\emph{Hũ majāmā chhũ, ābhār} — and to their thanks, \emph{vāndho nahĩ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
